content: Tick paralysis is a unique tick-borne disease that is not caused by an infectious organism. Instead, it results from a neurotoxin produced in the salivary glands of certain ticks. This toxin is transmitted to the host after prolonged attachment of the tick, particularly when the tick becomes engorged. The exact incidence of tick paralysis remains unknown. Signs and Symptoms Tick paralysis occurs when a neurotoxin from the tick's salivary glands is introduced into the host during a blood meal. Symptoms typically manifest within 2 to 7 days of tick attachment. The initial presentation is weakness in both legs, which progresses to paralysis. This paralysis ascends rapidly, affecting the trunk, arms, and head within hours. If untreated, it can lead to respiratory failure and death. In some cases, the disease may present as acute ataxia without muscle weakness. Patients may report minor sensory symptoms, but systemic signs are usually absent. Deep tendon reflexes are often diminished or absent. Ophthalmoplegia and bulbar palsy may also occur. Electromyographic (EMG) studies typically reveal a variable reduction in the amplitude of compound muscle action potentials, but repetitive nerve stimulation studies are usually normal. These findings suggest a failure of acetylcholine release at the motor nerve terminal. Subtle abnormalities in motor nerve conduction velocity and sensory action potentials may also be observed. Pathogenesis Tick paralysis is believed to result from toxins in the tick's saliva that enter the host's bloodstream during feeding. In North America, the most common ticks associated with this condition are the Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni) and the American dog tick (Dermacentor variabilis). Globally, 43 tick species have been implicated in human disease. In Australia, tick paralysis is caused by Ixodes holocyclus, with 20 fatal cases reported up to 1989. The condition has caused the deaths of thousands of animals, particularly cattle and sheep, worldwide. In the United States, tick paralysis is a concern for domestic animals and livestock, but human cases are rare and typically occur in children under 10 years of age. The condition arises when an engorged, gravid female tick produces a neurotoxin in its salivary glands and transmits it to the host during feeding. Experiments suggest that the highest toxin production occurs between the fifth and seventh day of attachment, often triggering or worsening symptoms. Unlike other tick-borne diseases such as Lyme disease, ehrlichiosis, and babesiosis, which are caused by systemic proliferation of parasites, tick paralysis is chemically induced and usually resolves once the tick is removed. However, in severe cases, profound paralysis can develop and may be fatal before the tick's presence is detected. Diagnostic Tests Diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms and the identification of an embedded tick, often found on the scalp. In the absence of a tick, the differential diagnosis includes Guillain-Barré syndrome and botulism. Differential Diagnosis Tick paralysis must be distinguished from other causes of muscle weakness, hypotonia, and flaccid paralysis. The differential diagnosis includes conditions such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, botulism, and other neuromuscular disorders. Treatment The primary treatment for tick paralysis is the removal of the embedded tick. This usually leads to resolution of symptoms within several hours to days. If the tick is not removed, the toxin can be fatal, with reported mortality rates of 10–12%, primarily due to respiratory paralysis. The tick should be removed by grasping it as close to the skin as possible and applying firm, steady pressure. Prevention Currently, no vaccine is available for tick-borne diseases, except for tick-borne encephalitis (TBE). Individuals should take precautions when entering tick-infested areas, especially during spring and summer. Preventive measures include avoiding overgrown trails, wearing light-colored clothing to make ticks more visible, and using long pants and closed-toe shoes. Tick repellents containing DEET (N,N-diethyl-m-toluamide) are only marginally effective and can be applied to skin or clothing. However, severe reactions to DEET-containing products can occur in some individuals, particularly young children. Permethrin, which can only be applied to clothing, is much more effective in preventing tick bites. Unlike DEET, permethrin is an insecticide that causes ticks to curl up and fall off treated clothing. Toxin Despite numerous attempts to isolate and identify the neurotoxin since its first isolation in 1966, the exact structure of the toxin remains unknown. The toxic component is believed to reside in the 40–80 kDa protein fraction.
